why: Count what fills one window: 5 sidebar items, 3 of them counted, 3 vessels, 3 people, 8 timed log rows that each name an owner, 4 deadlines citing the actual regulation and a countdown that ticks, with hierarchy built from mono timestamps, ink against grey and a solid-versus-dashed rail instead of cards or colour.

Pricing is a five-phase budget with a basis column instead of three tiers: a solid rule means the price is fixed, a dashed rule means it is an estimate, the totals reconcile ($4,800 + $1,350 = $6,150, plus $3,100 = $9,250, $6,771.91 billed) and the Approve button flips state and moves the header total.

A form is shown mid-draft, never empty: 7 filled fields, 4 casualty types with one selected, 3 named attachments and a narrative with tracked changes and a lawyer margin note, so the redline itself demonstrates the service, and the strike, insert and note animate in that order on entry.

Each of the 4 tabs opens a different document with its own structure (8-row checklist with dated proof, 6-row payment ledger, 4-step title chain, violation notice with a day counter and 3 response options), and the tablist is real: arrow keys, aria states and a 7 second progress line that auto-advances and pauses on hover.

Five features are shown as 5 unlike slices of one client file (text thread with a chartplotter drawn in inline SVG, month grid plus 7-row deadline list, 8-language roster, 8-line bill, 8 documents tagged by who may see them), and the 3+3 over 2+2+2 grid clips each slice at the tray edge so it reads as part of something larger.
